title: Many organic forms arise from uniform expansive growth limited by local constraints

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Many organic forms arise from uniform expansive growth limited by local constraints

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Many developmental changes of form are produced by local trammels or lines of constraint acting on otherwise uniform and symmetrical expansive growth, as a ligature turns a gourd into two globes or a muscular band makes the stomach a lopsided bubble.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It is clear, I think, that we may account for many ordinary biological processes of development or transformation of form by the existence of trammels or lines of constraint, which limit and determine the action of the expansive forces of growth that would otherwise be uniform and symmetrical.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVII, “On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms”; topic “Trammels and constrained growth”. Scope: development of tubular and vesicular organs (gut, stomach, heart, neural tube) and fruits

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch17-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.48

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern imaging can test selected organs and model alternatives, but constraint forces are mostly inferred and confounded with differential growth. The broad cross-organ claim is only partially covered.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map spatial growth rates and constraints during organ development, then compare a uniform-expansion-plus-local-constraints model with heterogeneous intrinsic growth models using held-out shape trajectories.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The word “many” lacks a denominator.

Datasets rarely measure forces and growth together.

Constraints and intrinsic growth heterogeneity can produce similar shapes.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.45

data adequacy: 0.32

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Particular illustrations, such as a banded stomach or a lobed heart, can be compared with images of adult organs. The claim is about the developmental process that produced them, and static anatomy is only a proxy. Because constraints can be placed after the fact, a fit does little to separate this account from other growth rules.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For organs such as the stomach, heart and gut, test whether shape matches a pressure vessel of uniform expansion plus localized constraints such as a muscular band, using the unconstrained vessel as the rival. Agreement at the named constrictions would support those examples; shapes that miss the constraint prediction would limit how many organs the account covers.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The word 'many' sets no quota of organs that must fit.

Adult shape is compatible with many developmental histories, so a geometric match does not show that growth was uniform expansion under a trammel.
